stories.headline: How Rays' unique approach carried Tampa Bay to World Series
stories.summary: The small-market Rays are kings of the American League. Here's what Tampa Bay does that nobody else can match.
stories.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Florida -- Self-awareness is the Tampa Bay Rays' superpower. A natural disaster tore the roof off their home, and their franchise player torpedoed his career in the ugliest manner imaginable, and never did the Rays fall prey to doubt. Baseball can be brutal and unrelenting and unforgiving, but when the world seemed to conspire against them, the Rays found solace in the one thing in which they never stopped believing: themselves.

Their trip to the 122nd World Series, booked with a rollicking 7-3 victory against the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night, crystallized the power of Tampa Bay's method and delivered madness to the 40,230 who filled Tropicana Field. Over the past two decades, the Rays had built something meaningful. Competing in a comically moneyed AL East, habitually dispossessed by comparison, the Rays leaned on that acute understanding of exactly who they are -- an organization that deifies a culture of questioning, improvement and accountability -- as their great equalizer. They stuck to these principles even after the demise of the career of Wander Franco, around whom they planned to build their franchise, and when damage to the Trop from Hurricane Milton forced them to a temporary home for the 2025 season.

And so through it all, the Rays did what the Rays always do, which is rely on a process honed through years of commitment to a single purpose: winning -- regardless of the impediments that exist.

"We have people that truly care about what they do," Rays president of baseball operations Erik Neander said. "Staff and players alike with a prevailing belief that we can win a championship here. A relentless pursuit of improvement by way of respecting all our differences and finding the good in each and everybody involved in this organization."

Neander leads a baseball operations department nearly 200 heads deep, and from it was born this group of 26, many of them misfit toys. Junior Caminero and Yandy Díaz, acquired in separate trades with the Guardians three years apart, supplied a pair of late-inning two-run home runs that provided the margin of victory. Freddy Peralta, secured in a deadline deal with the New York Mets in August, contributed 5 1⁄3 innings of high-octane pitching en route to ALCS MVP honors. Fifty-four innings of error-free baseball in the series reinforced that the Rays did not win the most games in the league by accident. They know who they are, and they spend every day seeking validation not for that but rather for what it breeds.

Which is a brand of baseball strikingly similar to that of their World Series opponent, the Milwaukee Brewers, the best team in the National League. The Rays and Brewers are baseball Rorschach tests. Some see them through the lens of their payrolls, 26th and 19th, respectively, and the size of their markets, 19th and 30th. That's too simple, though. The Rays and Brewers are not what they spend; they are what they produce, and that happens to be wondrous displays of baseball, from their multidimensional offensive approaches to their parade of arms that propel baseballs in manners that stretch the limits of the human body to the pride they take in minutiae, from defense to bunting to base stealing.

This World Series, in other words, is no accident, not some stroke of luck that will be painted as a battle of unlikelies. Doing so is a disservice to everything the Rays and Brewers are, which is proof that the power of money -- and suggesting it isn't an inherent advantage would be disingenuous-- has its limits. Namely, organizations that actively commingle the old and new, whether it's scouting and statistics or small ball and big flies. Without that ethos -- and without the certitude that it's right -- Caminero would not have been dancing on the field Monday night, holding a flag declaring the Rays AL champions.

It was not the first time Caminero inspired the Trop to ear-splitting decibels Monday, urged on by what was unfolding on the field. Up in the seventh inning against the Guardians' impermeable closer, Cade Smith, Caminero saw a split-fingered fastball boring inside and unfurled the fastest swing in the major leagues. Smith had thrown 884 splitters in his big league career without yielding a home run, only to see the 885th clang off the left-field foul pole.

Caminero went into showman mode, turning to his teammates and pounding his chest before touching first base. Nearly 40 seconds after his home run trot began, Caminero finished it by stopping a stride shy of home plate, turning toward the stands, pointing to one specific person and crossing his arms, full boss-mode.

He was looking at Randy Arozarena, the former Rays outfielder who hit a record 10 postseason home runs the last time Tampa Bay advanced to the World Series in 2020 and punctuated his best moments with that signature pose. Though he'd since been traded to Seattle, Arozarena wasn't going to miss this game, nor was Tyler Glasnow, the former Rays pitcher who had left in a deal to the Los Angeles Dodgers, winners of the past two World Series.

Once a Ray, always a Ray isn't some platitude. It is, perhaps, the foremost explanation of who they are and why they find themselves four wins from the first championship in franchise history.

Before the ninth inning of Game 6 began, Shane McClanahan found Yandy Díaz in the dugout and told him exactly where Díaz was going to hit a home run. The two are the most tenured members of the Rays, and even if dugout home run predictions are notoriously wrong, McClanahan felt something coming, a function of spending the last six seasons studying Díaz's consistent excellence.

"From Day 1, we've instilled it in every single person in this clubhouse," said McClanahan, who started the 2022 All-Star Game but is out for the postseason with left forearm tightness. "We're a team-first group. We're no egos. We play for each other, and we play hard. That's why he gave me that bear hug in the dugout at the end. I called the shot, man."

Losing a trade is painful enough -- and the Guardians unequivocally lost both deals with Tampa Bay. Caminero has turned from a rookie-ball flier into an MVP candidate. Díaz has posted the 10th-best on-base percentage in baseball since joining Tampa Bay in 2019. Losing a season to those who left in trades, as Cleveland just did, is insult, injury and indignity. And yet Caminero and Díaz comprise less than 8% of the Tampa Bay roster Neander and his band of dreamers constructed, so often via trades and unexpected signings.

Take Nick Martinez. Three days before spring training, the 36-year-old right-hander was unemployed. Tampa Bay, looking to expand its pitching depth, considered the array of available talent: future Hall of Famer Justin Verlander, veteran Chris Bassitt and right-hander Zack Littell, who, like many that go to the Rays, had demonstrably improved in his time there the prior two-plus seasons before being traded to Cincinnati at the 2025 deadline. When Neander reiterated the primary intention of any pitching signing -- "We are going to prioritize the one that's going to leave a lasting impression on their teammates," he told his group -- they kept gravitating back to Martinez.

He was, it turned out, an archetypal Ray despite never having worn navy and Columbia blue. Up at 23. Out of the league four years later and off to the Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters. Resurrected by four years in Japan before a return to the United States led to four solid seasons split between San Diego and Cincinnati. Because Martinez's fastball rarely exceeds 93 mph, teams let him rot in free agency until the Rays gave him a one-year, $13 million contract.

Their read on Martinez proved fortuitous. Pitchers gravitated toward him, as did hitters -- rare for clubhouses traditionally bifurcated by position. He spoke English and Spanish. He had lived a rich baseball life, full enough to serve as the glue that kept the Rays together, whether it was at a cigar bar or on a golf course or at copious team dinners that drew more than 20 teammates without fail.

"These guys make it easy, really," Martinez said. "They wanna hang. I can throw team dinners every week, and if no one shows up, no one shows up. These guys showed up. Camaraderie matters. It's a big part of our formula. The more you hang out with someone, the more you get to know someone. The more you get to know someone, the more you root for that person. We played for each other the whole season. We have no egos here. We just wanna do what the game asks of us and play for each other and celebrate together. We play very selfless baseball."

That manifested itself early. On April 18, the Rays faced Pittsburgh Pirates ace Paul Skenes and looked helpless through four scoreless innings. A rain delay of nearly 2½ hours followed, chasing Skenes and allowing Tampa Bay to chip away before winning 8-7 in 13 innings. In the aftermath of a long and perilous day, they stuck around in the clubhouse postgame, slugging beers, talking ball, a recurring theme throughout the season. The work of winning inside the white lines begins outside of them.

"This organization has a wonderful reputation of knowing how to win, how to get the best out of their guys," Martinez said. "They communicate the best I've ever been around. Tampa's always been on the list for me to come play for, and when they came calling, man, we ran with it."

By June 27, they captured a spot atop the AL East that they would not relinquish on their march to 98 wins. New heroes emerged daily. Cam Booser didn't even join the team until June and wound up one of the best relief pitchers in baseball and the personification of Tampa Bay's ability to help rescue what once was lost.

After five injury-riddled seasons in which he didn't advance past High-A, Booser retired in 2017 and went to work in construction. Four years later, when coaching kids in Washington, Booser realized he was still throwing in the high 90s from the left side and joined the independent Chicago Dogs, where he was scouted by Rays executive Kevin Ibach. While that gig didn't lead to a job in affiliated ball, Booser surfaced with the Boston Red Sox in 2024 and debuted at 32 years old before kicking around the last two years and finding a home in St. Petersburg.

"They make you feel special here, no matter who you are," Booser said. "They treat you all the same no matter who you are. If you're here, you're important. They take the time to invest in every single player, and they just believe in you. More than maybe you believe in yourself at the time. And that's infectious. They're consistent every single day. It's how they work. They trust the process no matter what, and you start to believe that."

Booser's belief came from the cluster of players he saw improving, compounded by the Rays' specific suggestions for his optimization. They wanted him to double down on the cutter he had thrown far less frequently the previous season. Booser knew Drew Rasmussen, the staff ace, and Griffin Jax, who arrived in a trade with Minnesota at the 2025 deadline. They couldn't say enough good things about the Rays.

"I understood they do things very differently here, in the best way possible," Booser said. "And I wanted to be a part of that."

He's not the only one. A common refrain throughout baseball is how many things the Rays do well, from scouting to drafting to international signing to player development. At the top of the list is taking an unlikely group and turning the players into productive big leaguers. Evaluators thought Jonathan Aranda was positionless with a bad body. He was an All-Star last year. Coming into this season, Ryan Vilade had played 28 big league games with four teams. The Rays recognized he crushed left-handed pitching and leaned on him in 96 games this year as a platoon specialist. The Guardians cast aside Richie Palacios after taking him in the third round of the 2018 MLB draft. He resurfaced with the Rays and batted .500 in the ALCS with a two-run double in Game 6 that staked the Rays a 2-0 advantage.

"They have a unique way of making guys feel very comfortable with who they are," said Rays shortstop Taylor Walls, who, despite poor offensive performance, maintains the starting job because the Rays so deeply value his defense. "When guys enter the organization, they can sense that people really have their back, that they can really be themselves and not be afraid to make mistakes, to really just be great at what they're great at and not try to do anything else outside of that. And I think it really allows guys to find out who they are, to give themselves an identity and just to buy in."

Buying in wasn't a problem for Peralta, who joined catcher Liam Hicks and Booser's co-setup man, Tyler Wells, as the Rays' deadline acquisitions. Peralta, 30, spent his first eight years with the Brewers until they dealt him to the New York Mets over the winter, one season before he was due to hit free agency. As the Mets crumbled, so did Peralta. After Tampa Bay snagged him at the deadline for three minor leaguers, coaches and other staff sat with him in Colorado and "were very clear with me. They told me, 'We know who you are. We know what you have done and your whole career. We're not looking at the last three months of your career. We know who you are, and we're gonna help you to get your confidence back.' And, you know, in the moment, I believed them."

The belief was warranted. The Rays wanted Peralta to throw his devastating changeup more often, and with it came an uptick in his fastball velocity. In his last six regular-season starts, he posted a 0.79 ERA in 34 innings. In 12 innings spread over two starts and one relief appearance in the ALCS, Peralta allowed one run, winning Games 2 and 6, capturing the hardware to match his NLCS MVP counterpart, Jake Bauers -- who the Rays traded in 2018 in a deal to get Díaz. Offering substantive advice, scraping for marginal value, endlessly trying to get better -- the Rays' way was familiar, and comfortable, to Peralta for good reason.

"It's very similar," he said, "to Milwaukee."

Self-awareness is not just about knowing what you are. It's recognizing what you aren't, and, in that respect, the Rays and Brewers are kindred spirits. The same inequities that limit the Rays constrain the Brewers, and it's what makes this World Series so tantalizing: The parties occupy similar ground.

The Brewers have not made the World Series in 44 years and have not captured a championship in their 58 years of existence. The Rays lost in both of their previous World Series appearances -- falling to Philadelphia in 2008 and Los Angeles in 2020 -- and are title-free for 29 seasons. There will be a first-time World Series winner this year, amplifying the stakes -- and the crowds at American Family Field, where Game 1 begins Friday with Brewers ace and soon-to-be NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski against Rasmussen.

For all of the narrative to come about the grand meaning of the Rays and Brewers facing barely a month before the league is set to lock out the players who won't agree to a salary cap the league has positioned as necessary to help small-market teams, this World Series is, as much as anything, a pure display of the game, a collision of the present with the past.

It already was evident with the Rays, even as they clinched. They wore Devil Rays jerseys, a vestige of their early years. The Caminero-Arozarena exchange was generational aura. Even the team's past leadership was present, with former team president Matt Silverman joining Patrick Zalupski, Bill Cosgrove and Ken Babby, the new ownership group that bought the team in September 2025 and intends to replace the aged Trop with a new stadium in Tampa.

The Rays' stability, in part, has come from their ability to complement their longtime employees with new faces to replace those who left the Tampa Bay machine and eventually took over other baseball operations departments: Andrew Friedman (Dodgers), Chaim Bloom (Boston and St. Louis), Peter Bendix (Miami), James Click (Houston), Taylor Smith (A's) and Matt Arnold, who runs the Brewers. The Rays' fingerprints are everywhere in baseball.

"Since I was drafted at 17, every coach that I've been with, the players they drafted, you could tell that everybody was just a straight-up A-plus human being," Walls said. "And if they weren't, they got out. You've got to be a good person to be in this organization. You gotta care about winning. Winning has to be your only priority. And if it's not, they sniff you out real quick and you're probably not here long."

Plenty do stay. Scout Mitch Lukevics joined the Rays three years before they debuted in 1998 and hasn't left. As teams across the industry have cut scouting jobs, Ibach has bulked up the Rays' department with trusted pro personnel specialists Mike Brown, Max Cohen, Jason Cole, Jaosn Grey, Nate Howard and Mike Langill. They're the rare big league organization featuring multiple women in high-ranking baseball-operations positions, with assistant GM Chanda Lawdermilk, director of position player programming Dani Dockx and director of baseball operations Sammi Bireley, who has been pulling double duty to graduate recently from law school. Jon Daniels, the general manager of two Texas Rangers World Series teams, found refuge with Tampa Bay. Super-scout Bobby Heck did the same after Houston whacked its scouting department. Jeff Sullivan, the longtime FanGraphs wordsmith, is eight years into a multipurpose role with the organization. The Rays this year hired three former big leaguers -- Mike Ford, Beau Sulser and Joe Hudson -- to seed the next generation of front office talent. The pipeline doesn't run dry because Neander and his other deputies, Hamilton Marx and Will Cousins, refuse to let it.

All of them, and plenty more, deserve to be named because, as Booser said, "all our success is just a credit to our front office." And to Kevin Cash, the manager who guides the fruits of that labor with pitching coach Kyle Snyder and hitting coach Chad Mottola. They are the ticking heart of Tampa Bay's operation, the ones who made playing in a minor league park in 2025 palatable while the Trop was undergoing Extreme Makeover: Stadium Edition, the ones who have brought calm no matter the challenge.

Now Caminero and Diaz are swatting balls for the Rays instead of against them, Walls is picking balls no other shortstop would reach, and Chandler Simpson is burning around the basepaths faster than anyone in the big leagues. Rasmussen did snow angels in the confetti strewn about the Trop's turf after Hicks squeezed the final out of the ALCS, secured by All-Star closer Bryan Baker, who was acquired from Baltimore for the 37th overall draft pick in a 2025 trade. It was a proper celebration for a proper team that knows exactly what it is. How the rest of the world sees it will depend on the next 11 days, but after Monday, at least one thing is no longer in question: The Rays are, as they've been for most of the year, the class of the AL.

As for all of baseball, the 103-win Brewers might have something to say about that. They'll get a chance to on the field. The Rays' self-awareness extends to the World Series, and they understand just how good their opponent is, but that doesn't disabuse them of a core tenet that won't go away anytime soon.

They believe.

stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of F1 history -- but first, there's a car to wash and pranks to pull
stories.summary: On the brink of becoming F1's youngest world champion, Kimi Antonelli reveals how car washes, pub trips and pranks help him cope with fame and pressure.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli likes to make sure his car is clean.

Even before a trip that is likely to end with him becoming Formula 1's youngest world champion, he cannot bring himself to leave before he's completed a familiar ritual: a visit to the car wash in his road car, a Mercedes GT63. The Italian washes it by hand, meticulously, inside and out. Only then can he travel to his next Formula 1 race.

Asked whether or not he times himself at the car wash, 20-year-old Antonelli laughed.

"No, no, no," he replied in a small group interview including ESPN.

"I take my time because it needs to be done well. It needs to be cleaned well. It needs to be dried well, because if you don't dry it well and there's still some water [on it], then, you know, it's weird. It looks dirty. So it needs to be done well and then also inside.

"I take my time. For that, I take my time."

- How Antonelli can win F1 title at U.S. Grand Prix

- Horner: Hamilton keen on Red Bull before Merc move

It's funny, because almost nothing about Antonelli's journey to this point has been an exercise in taking one's time.

The U.S. Grand Prix on Oct. 26 will be the first time in his career he can win the Formula 1 world drivers' championship, even if there's only a slim mathematical chance he will get it done at the Circuit of the Americas. But whether he does it there, or in Mexico City a week later, or in Brazil a week after that, or at the triple header currently slated to finish the season, Antonelli's lead is so big that he almost certainly will at some point in the next two months become the sport's youngest-ever world champion, in just his second season racing in Formula 1. Amid all of that, keeping any semblance of normality has been a challenge in itself.

Which brings us back to the car wash.

"Racing is always on my mind. I try not to think too much about, first of all, the situation I'm in, because I feel like if I would think too much about championship and stuff, I would probably get anxious as well. Also I wouldn't have quality time at home, because I would just be worrying about this."

He then elaborated on his new-found ritual.

"I like to clean my car," Antonelli said. "I never do automatic, you know, with the machine. I always like to wash by hand, myself. Because I love cars, I really like to take care of my car and everything. I like to see it clean, so it's an activity I love to do. It's a routine."

Normality and routine has been the name of the game for Antonelli in 2026 as he has tried to fight off the growing realisation of what he's about to achieve. But it has been difficult. He's become a superstar in Italy, almost overnight, with his legendary status at home cemented in September with his astonishing victory from 19th on the grid at the Italian Grand Prix. It made him the first Italian winner of that race since 1966 and will go down as the crowning moment of a season which will end with him becoming the first Italian world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953. A nation so regularly tortured by Ferrari's disappointments over the past two decades has had a singular new star to rally around.

That would be a lot for anyone to shoulder -- let alone someone who had only turned 20 two weeks before he stood on the top step of Monza's iconic podium stage.

Asked how he has processed becoming Italy's biggest sporting icon so young, he shrugged, and shook his head, almost as if still unable to fully comprehend it all.

"I try to realise the least as possible," he said. "The situation I'm in, and also the person I'm becoming ... whenever I go back home, I want to feel as normal as possible."

Key to that has been Antonelli's school friends -- the same he studied with last year, when his mother insisted that he had to finish his exams even if he had become a Formula 1 rookie at 18. The same friends who came to support him in the paddock at the Imola race, a stone's throw away from hometown Bologna, last year.

"The situation I'm in and also the person I'm becoming ... whenever I go back home, I want to feel as normal as possible," he said. "I always try to do the normal things, like every human being. So, go to the supermarket, go, to the cinema ... it's more difficult, but I still do so.

"I go with my friends to the pub to watch sport. Especially when we have a weekend off and there's racing, or there's tennis, or any kind of sport. I like to go to the pub with my friends and watch from there, or play bowling, this kind of stuff.

"Whenever I go back home, I try to live a normal life. Of course, it's not easy at times, because whenever you go, it's harder to get the same amount of privacy."

Antonelli's claims of trips to the car wash, the pub, the supermarket and bowling alley would be harder to fathom if he lived in the big city or in a bustling modern town, given the harsh combination of his enormous fame and the social media age he's grown into. While most of his F1 rivals live in Monaco, he now resides in San Marino, the small republic housed inside Italy, about 80 miles from Bologna.

"I like San Marino because it's very small and basically everyone knows each other. You don't get asked for pictures anymore because it's always the same people. I think it's really cool.

"But yeah, whenever I go back home, I just try to live a normal life, not think too much about racing and just enjoy the time with my friends, family, because it also helps me to disconnect a little bit and especially get out from this external bubble that we are in, especially when we're at the race weekend."

From raw rookie to F1 superstar
It seemed to be an enormous gamble, to put it mildly, when Mercedes boss Toto Wolff decided that the man to replace the Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, F1's most accomplished driver, in 2025 should in fact be a teenager. Antonelli, the exciting, but untested prodigy on Mercedes' junior programme, was given the nod.

The narrative that it was too much too soon was easy to write -- Antonelli crashed out of his first practice run at Monza in August 2024, a day before the team made the official confirmation. Wolff later admitted the free practice appearance in front of a frenzied Italian media and fanbase had been ill-advised. After that crash, Mercedes' boss gave his viewpoint on Antonelli's raw, then-unpolished talent, one he has repeated in some form or another a lot over the next two years: "It's always easier to calm down a fast horse than to make a slow horse fast."

Wolff and Mercedes had to echo that viewpoint a lot in 2025. Antonelli's rookie season was a rollercoaster -- especially in a dismal run of European races in the middle of the year, which included a collision with Max Verstappen in Austria and Charles Leclerc in the Netherlands -- and the stark contrast to teammate George Russell's superb and consistent performances in the other car made it easy to anoint the British driver as preseason favourite coming into a new season and rules set which re-established Mercedes as the benchmark team to beat. But Antonelli went into the winter break with a chance to take stock at the opportunity he had been given.

"It was mainly digesting. The first season, you're naturally a bit more tense," he said.

"I felt like I mainly needed time, to digest, to look at the season again. Understand what was good about the season, what was not good. And understanding as well, what was good for me."

Antonelli, who has admitted he tried to do too much as a rookie, both on and off track, came into the new season a changed man. After Russell won the opening race in Australia, Antonelli claimed an emotional maiden win in China and then won the next four in a row in Japan, Miami, Canada and Monaco. He's not looked back since. He snuffed out a brief Russell fightback by winning in Belgium in July, before the Italy win was followed up by victory at Madring's first Spanish Grand Prix.

Even to Antonelli, the contrast between life as an overthinking rookie and a championship leader is night and day.

"It's pretty insane, the step," he admitted. "Because, for sure, having a fast car helps. Obviously. [But] I wouldn't have expected to be a contender like this, this season. Of course, I find myself in this position and I'm very happy, very grateful to be in this position and I've got to keep pushing.

"But ... definitely, at the start of the year, I would have never thought to be in this position. Especially because we were confident with the car, I knew I could have fought for wins. A few wins, podiums. But to be in this position? For sure not. But it was a very nice surprise.

"And now we've just got to finish the job."

He pointed to the Monza victory as the best example of how he's changed things.

"Last year, at the home race, the way it was managed was not good. The way I managed myself. While this year, I feel like, on things that are less important, I leant a lot on the people that I have around [me]. So they take care of it and I don't have to worry about [those things].

"The only thing I worry about is going on track and doing the best I can. While last year, I was worrying about way too many things. Especially my home race. And that's why I felt so drained, mentally, so early into the weekend.

"While this year, I feel in a much better place. Much more protected. Also because the things that I tried to take care of last year, this year the team was taking care of, the people working with me. I could focus on the important things. That has been a big thing for me."

The prankster world champion
Those close to Antonelli will all tell you the same thing: becoming F1's newest superstar has not changed him at all. Antonelli's happy-go-lucky approach to life seemed perfect for a teenage rookie -- but many at Mercedes wondered how long that would last through his elevation to a championship contender.

But rather than becoming a pressure-cooker environment, things have flipped around, something he said he notices in how he interacts with race engineer Peter Bonnington, who works with Antonelli now having guided Hamilton to his six championships at Mercedes.

"This is more relaxed," he said. "You have more confidence with the team. You know each other better. Last year, for example, with Bono.

"As an Italian, I like to give hugs. For example, after a race, after a great result, I like to go there and give him a hug. Share the moment. And last year, it would get very tense at times. You could see it would tense up. But this year, he actually enjoys it. Because he knows it's part of myself as well.

"But also, he enjoys it. He probably won't admit it, but he does. He does enjoy it."

Bonnington has been on the receiving end of a lot of Antonelli's mischief this year -- the team's Instagram account has recorded several pranks at the race engineer's expense, including Antonelli putting chilli sauce in his drink during preseason testing, and having his key card for Mercedes' F1 headquarters turned off during a visit ahead of the summer break.

Antonelli's boyish enthusiasm for japes has extended to the whole team. After the summer break, a fake interview was set up by the team in the paddock, giving 19 mechanics an opportunity to ambush the Italian and cover him in plates of cream.

During our interview, Antonelli started laughing and briefly asked to go off record so he could detail his next devious plan.

He then ran through a list of people who have been on the receiving end through the season, but there was one obvious name missing.

Asked if he has ever dared prank Wolff, Antonelli laughed.

The young man on the verge of achieving the biggest thing in all of motor racing admitted he still needs to work up the courage for that.

"This is next level," he said in reply. "You need to have big balls to do that!"

Of course, Antonelli might just have the confidence needed to do it by the end of the year.

"I'm going to have to finish well in the championship, finish well this year. Then I have a reason to do it [to Wolff].

"And so then he won't complain too much about it! But that's like next level."

stories.headline: Petr Yan vs. Merab Dvalishvili joins rare list of trilogy bouts at UFC 333
stories.summary: ESPN categorizes all 19 of the UFC's trilogies ahead of Petr Yan vs. Merab Dvalishvili 3 at UFC 333 on Saturday.
stories.body:
When men's bantamweight champion Petr Yan and former champion Merab Dvalishvili fight in the UFC 333 co-main event on Saturday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, it will be their third meeting, completing the promotion's 20th trilogy.

This weekend's headliners, featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski and undefeated challenger Movsar Evloev, will square off for the first time, but Volkanovski has already been part of a UFC trilogy. His threepeat with Max Holloway several years ago played out far differently from what will unfold in the UFC 333 co-main. That's guaranteed. (Read on to find out why.)

How fitting is it that Saturday's event is numbered 333, a coincidental acknowledgment that when the UFC deals out three of a kind, the fans end up with a winning hand. Usually.

Trilogies come in all shapes with all sizes. Many of the sport's biggest stars have been in one or more, yet at least one UFC three-fight series featured competitors newer fans probably haven't heard of. Some trilogies have had championship-level stakes in each fight, while others have been driven by nothing but a scornful rivalry that makes the fights feel no less consequential. A few trilogies have been one-sided and a couple have concluded without establishing who's better. We did the math.

Other MMA organizations have staged trilogies, and some have played out across multiple promotions, but this list sticks to the 19 all-UFC trilogies to date and sorts them by similarities and distinguishing factors.

Passing the torch
Trilogies in which the winner of the first fight was at the top of the sport, and by the third meeting the opponent was MMA's top fighter

Chuck Liddell vs. Randy Couture
Results:

UFC 43, June 6, 2003: Couture def. Liddell (TKO3) for interim light heavyweight title
UFC 52, April 16, 2005: Liddell def. Couture (KO1) for light heavyweight title
UFC 57, Feb. 4, 2006: Liddell def. Couture (KO2) for light heavyweight title

Notable: In the lead-up to their second meeting, Liddell and Couture coached against each other on the inaugural season of "The Ultimate Fighter," the reality show UFC CEO Dana White often credits with keeping the UFC in business. Through their TV appearances and contrasting fighting styles and personalities, Liddell and Couture helped catapult MMA toward the sports mainstream. Couture is one of just three fighters (along with Tito Ortiz and Matt Hughes) to compete in two UFC trilogies -- this one and a trio of fights with Vitor Belfort.

Georges St-Pierre vs. Matt Hughes
Results:

UFC 50, Oct. 22, 2004: Hughes def. St-Pierre (Sub1) for welterweight title
UFC 65, Nov. 18, 2006: St-Pierre def. Hughes (TKO2) for welterweight title
UFC 79, Dec. 29, 2007: St-Pierre def. Hughes (Sub2) for interim welterweight title

Notable: This is the only UFC trilogy to feature multiple submission finishes. Hughes won by armbar at UFC 50, and St-Pierre ended the trilogy at UFC 79 by submitting Hughes, also by armbar. When the fighters were standing, though, GSP dominated. In their second meeting, he outstruck Hughes 49-10 with two knockdowns. In the third fight, it was 97-10.

A stunning start ... and finish
Trilogies that began with a shocking KO upset, followed by the KO victim scoring two dominant wins

Cain Velasquez vs. Junior Dos Santos
Results:

UFC on Fox, Nov. 12, 2011: Dos Santos def. Velasquez (KO1) for heavyweight title
UFC 155, Dec. 29, 2012: Velasquez def. Dos Santos (UD) for heavyweight title
UFC 166, Oct. 19, 2013: Velasquez def. Dos Santos (TKO5) for heavyweight title

Notable: The first fight lasted barely a minute, as Dos Santos essentially won by one-punch knockout. The rematch and trilogy fight dramatically swung the other way. Velasquez battered JDS for the full 25 minutes of their second meeting, as reflected by one judge awarding him two 10-8 rounds. Velasquez became the first UFC fighter to reach triple-figure significant strikes (111) and double-figure takedowns (11) in a single fight.

Stipe Miocic vs. Daniel Cormier
Results:

UFC 226, July 7, 2018: Cormier def. Miocic (KO1) for heavyweight title
UFC 241, Aug. 17, 2019: Miocic def. Cormier (TKO4) for heavyweight title
UFC 252, Aug. 15, 2020: Miocic def. Cormier (UD) for heavyweight title

Notable: Cormier was light heavyweight champion when he first faced Miocic, and by crushing the heavyweight king with an uppercut, Cormier became the second UFC champ to reign in two weight classes simultaneously. Miocic bounced back in the next two fights, and his victory in the third meeting tied him with Couture for the most UFC heavyweight title-fight wins, with six.

Back and forth (and back)
Trilogies in which the winner of the first fight lost the second, then won the third -- a rarity

Randy Couture vs. Vitor Belfort
Results:

UFC 15, Oct. 17, 1997: Couture def. Belfort (TKO1)
UFC 46, Jan. 31, 2004: Belfort def. Couture (TKO1) for light heavyweight title
UFC 49, Aug. 21, 2004: Couture def. Belfort (TKO3) for light heavyweight title

Notable: Entering the first fight, Belfort was 20 years old and 4-0 as a pro -- all knockouts of a minute, 17 seconds or faster. But Couture, 34, stopped his momentum cold. When they met again six years later, Belfort won in 49 seconds after his glove scraped Couture's eye, causing a corneal abrasion that prompted the cageside doctor to stop the fight. In the third fight, Couture brutalized Belfort for three rounds before that event's doctor had seen enough. This is the only UFC trilogy in which two fights ended by doctor's stoppage.

BJ Penn vs. Matt Hughes
Results:

UFC 46, Jan. 31, 2004: Penn def. Hughes (Sub1) for welterweight title
UFC 63, Sept. 23, 2006: Hughes def. Penn (TKO3) for welterweight title
UFC 123, Nov. 20, 2010: Penn def. Hughes (KO1)

Notable: After two unsuccessful bids for the lightweight championship, Penn moved up to welterweight and won the belt in a stunning upset, ending Hughes' two-year reign and 13-fight winning streak. After Hughes won the rematch to even the score, Penn completed the trilogy in style, knocking out Hughes in 21 seconds -- the fastest finish in a UFC trilogy.

You're just flexing now
Trilogies that ended in a 3-0 sweep

Tito Ortiz vs. Ken Shamrock
Results:

UFC 40, Nov. 12, 2002: Ortiz def. Shamrock (TKO3) for light heavyweight title
UFC 61, July 8, 2006: Ortiz def. Shamrock (TKO1)
UFC Ortiz vs. Shamrock 3, Oct. 10, 2006: Ortiz def. Shamrock (TKO1)

Notable: This trilogy is unmatched in its bitter animosity, for sure, and maybe even in one-sidedness. The feud grew out of the brash Ortiz defeating fighters from Shamrock's highly regarded Lion's Den gym, then mocking that team with vulgar gestures and custom T-shirts. Ortiz and Shamrock finally met at UFC 40 amid much anticipation, and the heated buildup drove a pay-per-view buy rate double what the UFC had ever seen.

Frankie Edgar vs. BJ Penn
Results:

UFC 112, April 10, 2010: Edgar def. Penn (UD) for lightweight title
UFC 118, Aug. 28, 2010: Edgar def. Penn (UD) for lightweight title
The Ultimate Fighter 19 Finale, July 6, 2014: Edgar def. Penn (TKO3)

Notable: Penn, who had not lost a lightweight bout in eight years, was a near 8-1 betting favorite in the first fight. Even after Edgar pulled off a narrow upset, he was still the underdog entering the rematch. He won that one more clearly with three 50-45 scorecards, then completed the trilogy with a knockout. Of the UFC's 19 trilogies, 11 have ended with a finish in the third fight. But only two -- both involving Edgar -- ended with a finish after two consecutive decisions. The other was Edgar's series with Gray Maynard.

Alexander Volkanovski vs. Max Holloway
Results:

UFC 245, Dec. 14, 2019: Volkanovski def. Holloway (UD) for featherweight title
UFC 251, July 11, 2020: Volkanovski def. Holloway (SD) for featherweight title
UFC 276, July 2, 2022: Volkanovski def. Holloway (UD) for featherweight title

Notable: Just because this trilogy ended 3-0 doesn't mean Volkanovski had it easy. In the second fight, Holloway knocked him down in each of the first two rounds, forcing the champ to play catch-up. Holloway made Volkanovski work the full five rounds in all three fights. At 75 minutes of total cage time, this is the UFC's longest trilogy.

Let's call it even
Trilogies that ended at 1-1, plus a draw

Frankie Edgar vs. Gray Maynard
Results:

UFC Fight Night, April 2, 2008: Maynard def. Edgar (UD)
UFC 125, Jan. 1, 2011: Maynard vs. Edgar for lightweight title ends in split draw
UFC 136, Oct. 8, 2011: Edgar def. Maynard (KO4) for lightweight title

Notable: The second meeting produced the greatest comeback and the most memorable draw in UFC history. Maynard knocked Edgar down three times in Round 1 while piling up a 47-10 edge in strikes landed. All three judges scored it 10-8, and Edgar was so rocked that he doesn't remember anything from the rounds that followed. He "missed" a great fight. The final meeting also began badly for Edgar, but this time his comeback built toward a late knockout that emphatically evened the score.

Valentina Shevchenko vs. Alexa Grasso
Results:

UFC 285, March 4, 2023: Grasso def. Shevchenko (Sub4) for women's flyweight title
Noche UFC, Sept. 16, 2023: Shevchenko vs. Grasso for women's flyweight title ends in split draw
UFC 306, Sept. 14, 2024: Shevchenko def. Grasso (UD) for women's flyweight title

Notable: The only women's trilogy in UFC history opened with a staggering upset, as Grasso capitalized on an ill-advised spinning attack by Shevchenko to seize control and quickly lock in a choke that ended the champ's six-year unbeaten run. Grasso narrowly held on to the title in a tightly contested second fight. Shevchenko dominated the third meeting, thanks to a change in strategy. Her grappling-heavy approach produced at least one takedown in each of the five rounds, 16 minutes of ground control and a trio of 50-45 scorecards.

Remember me?
Trilogies with at least seven years between fights

Dustin Poirier vs. Max Holloway
Results:

UFC 143, Feb. 4, 2012: Poirier def. Holloway (Sub1) for interim lightweight title
UFC 236, April 13, 2019: Poirier def. Holloway (UD)
UFC 318, July 19, 2025: Holloway def. Poirier (UD) for BMF title

Notable: The first fight was Holloway's UFC debut at 20 years old, and their final meeting 13 years later was Poirier's retirement fight. By winning that third bout, Holloway became the first fighter to win a UFC trilogy after losing the first two matchups.

Leon Edwards vs. Kamaru Usman
Results:

UFC on Fox, Dec. 19, 2015: Usman def. Edwards (UD)
UFC 278, Aug. 20, 2022: Edwards def. Usman (KO5) for welterweight title
UFC 268, March 18, 2023: Edwards def. Usman (MD) for welterweight title

Notable: Usman was 58 seconds from going up 2-0 in this series when an Edwards head kick out of nowhere changed everything. Usman had won 15 fights in a row and was on the verge of tying Anderson Silva's record for the longest UFC win streak at the time. Since that shocking defeat, he's gone 1-3, including another loss to Edwards.

No gold, just (a little) glory
Trilogies in which no championships were on the line

Sam Stout vs. Spencer Fisher
Results:

UFC 58, March 4, 2006: Stout def. Fisher (SD)
UFC Fight Night, June 12, 2007: Fisher def. Stout (UD)
UFC on FX, June 22, 2012: Stout def. Fisher (UD)

Notable: The first meeting was Stout's UFC debut, and apparently both fighters were just warming up. The rematch and trilogy fight each earned fight of the night bonuses. The third meeting had an added emotional element for Stout, as it was his first fight after the death of his coach and brother-in-law, Shawn Tompkins.

Forrest Griffin vs. Tito Ortiz
Results:

UFC 59, April 15, 2006: Ortiz def. Griffin (SD)
UFC 106, Nov. 21, 2009: Griffin def. Ortiz (SD)
UFC 148, July 7, 2012: Griffin def. Ortiz (UD)

Notable: Both competitors were 205-pound champions, just not during any of their three meetings. All three fights happened after Ortiz's title reign from 2000 to 2003. The first fight was before Griffin became champ in 2008, and the other two were after he lost the belt later that same year. The trilogy fight was Griffin's career finale and Ortiz's final UFC appearance.

Charles Oliveira vs. Nik Lentz
Results:

UFC on Versus, June 26, 2011: Oliveira vs. Lentz ends in no contest
UFC Fight Night, May 30, 2015: Oliveira def. Lentz (Sub3)
UFC Fight Night, May 18, 2019: Oliveira def. Lentz (TKO2)

Notable: The first bout appeared to end with an Oliveira rear-naked choke in Round 2, but the Pennsylvania State Athletic Commission ruled that Oliveira had landed an illegal knee and overturned the result to a no-contest. The bout earned both men fight of the night bonuses, as did the second fight.

Dustin Poirier vs. Conor McGregor
Results:

UFC 178, Sept. 27, 2014: McGregor def. Poirier (TKO1)
UFC 257, Jan. 23, 2021: Poirier def. McGregor (TKO2)
UFC 264, July 10, 2021: Poirier def. McGregor (TKO1)

Notable: This rivalry could have fit in the "Remember me?" category because of the seven-year gap between the first and second bouts. But what truly makes this trilogy stand apart from all others is McGregor's star power. He headlined the seven highest-selling pay-per-views in UFC history, and only his bouts with Khabib Nurmagomedov and Nate Diaz outsold his two meetings with Poirier in 2021. McGregor suffered the first two knockout losses of his MMA career in those bouts, the second finish coming by doctor's stoppage after he broke his left tibia and fibula.

Three is not enough?
The only UFC tetralogy -- plus 75% of another

Brandon Moreno vs. Deiveson Figueiredo
Results:

UFC 256, Dec. 12, 2020: Moreno vs. Figueiredo for men's flyweight title ends in majority draw
UFC 263, June 12, 2021: Moreno def. Figueiredo (Sub3) for men's flyweight title
UFC 270, Jan. 22, 2022: Figueiredo def. Moreno (UD) for men's flyweight title
UFC 283, Jan. 21, 2023: Moreno def. Figueiredo (TKO3) for men's flyweight title

Notable: These two flyweights squeezed in four fights over 25 months, faster than many two-fight series. Moreno and Figueiredo each produced heart-pounding moments throughout the four fights, and together they landed exactly 700 strikes. The second fight represented a memorable accomplishment for Moreno when he became the first Mexico-born UFC champion.

Tim Sylvia vs. Andrei Arlovski
Results:

UFC 51, Feb. 5, 2005: Arlovski def. Sylvia (Sub1) for interim heavyweight title
UFC 59, April 15, 2006: Sylvia def. Arlovski (TKO1) for heavyweight title
UFC 61, July 8, 2006: Sylvia def. Arlovski (UD) for heavyweight title
One FC 5, Aug. 31, 2012: Sylvia vs. Arlovski ends no contest in One Championship

Notable: The first fight lasted 47 seconds, with Arlovski's quick knockdown leading to a leg-lock finish. Arlovski nearly repeated the feat in the rematch, dropping Sylvia halfway through Round 1. But after a wobbly Sylvia got back to his feet and Arlovski moved in for a finish, Sylvia caught him with a short uppercut to even the score. Their final UFC meeting turned into a tactical, tentative sparring session, as one might expect from a matchup where each fighter had already felt the other's power. Also as expected, the ornery crowd was unimpressed.

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1. Isaac Issa has news from the Dragons on some key outside backs
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return

Jeral Skelton is closing in on a return to Canterbury following his departure from the Wests Tigers.

ESPN understands the Bulldogs are in advanced discussions to bring the outside back to the club for the 2027 season.

An agreement is understood to be close, although the deal has yet to be finalised.

Multiple NRL sides eye Knights forward

A Sydney club and a Queensland-based club are monitoring Newcastle forward Mat Croker ahead of November 1.

ESPN understands the two clubs have shown interest in the 27-year-old, who is approaching the final year of his Knights contract and can negotiate with rivals for 2028 onwards from next month.

Rivals keeping tabs on Dragons' Tu

Multiple clubs are monitoring St George Illawarra outside back Setu Tu, with the Dragons yet to begin talks over a contract extension.

Tu is contracted until the end of 2027 and is expected to test the open market from November 1, when rival clubs can negotiate a deal for 2028 and beyond.

The former Warriors outside back joined the Dragons on a development contract this season and is set to move into the club's top 30 squad in 2027.

His ability to cover multiple positions across the backline adds to his appeal as clubs assess their recruitment options.

Rivals monitor Patea as open market looms
Penrith young gun Luron Patea is expected to test the open market from November 1, with multiple clubs keeping tabs on the promising prop.

Patea is contracted until the end of 2027, but the Panthers are yet to begin talks over an extension, leaving rival clubs poised to explore a deal for 2028 and beyond.

Penrith have not granted Patea permission to negotiate with other clubs before November 1.

The Panthers junior made his NRL debut in 2024 and has shown promise during his first-grade opportunities, providing another emerging option in Penrith's forward pack.

He is among several Panthers players approaching the final year of their contracts, with veteran prop Moses Leota also unsigned beyond 2027.

Roosters eye Dockar-Clay reunion
The Roosters have shown interest in a potential return for Zach Dockar-Clay as they explore options to bolster their hooking and utility depth.

ESPN understands the 31-year-old has emerged as an option following his departure from Manly, with discussions remaining at an early stage.

Dockar-Clay spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons with the Roosters before joining the Sea Eagles on a one-year deal for 2026.

Manly confirmed his departure last month after a season in which he claimed the club's NSW Cup best-and-fairest award.

Bostock brushes Dragons links

Dolphins star Jack Bostock has dismissed recent links between himself and the Dragons, admitting this isn't the first time he'd been floated for a club switch.

"I've been linked to a few a clubs," Bostock admitted.

"I don't know about [the Dragons links]."

He said that while he "obviously sees it in the media," his sole focus is the Kangaroos.

Sloan's Dragons stay still a possibility

Tyrell Sloan could yet remain at St George Illawarra next season, with discussions ongoing over a potential stay despite his planned move to Castleford.

There is interest in keeping Sloan at the Dragons, but several hurdles remain before that can become a reality.

Roster space and salary cap room would need to be worked through, while any arrangement would also require Castleford to agree to release him.

Sloan previously admitted he would "love to" remain in the NRL when speaking to Channel Nine in August, after his Castleford deal had been announced.

No agreement has been reached and a stay is far from guaranteed.
